title: How a Leader's Oversized Ego Influences Their Behavior
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Notes entry defines ego as a leader's sense of self and the instinct to protect it, and says every leader has one. A healthy ego supplies confidence and courage, but an unchecked one pushes personal recognition, control and status ahead of the organization and its people. The author lists the recognisable signs of an oversized ego: a strong need to be right, a need for control that shows up as micromanaging, a hunger for credit, a fear of looking weak that leads to hiding mistakes, and a retreat into title and status. He adds that insecure leaders feel threatened when team members excel and may withhold opportunities from them. The closing claim is that a leader's greatest challenge is managing self rather than others, because leaders exist to support the organization and not the reverse.
points: Ego is framed as neither good nor bad in itself, since a healthy measure gives a leader the conviction to make hard decisions.
Needing to be right shows up as dismissing opposing views, justifying poor decisions and treating disagreement as disloyalty.
A need for control produces micromanagement and discourages independent thinking, because the leader confuses leadership with control over people.
Fear of appearing weak makes leaders hide mistakes and avoid asking for help, while insecurity makes them withhold opportunities from talented team members.
The test of true leadership is direction of service: leaders exist to support the organization and its people, and anything else is just the ego talking.
quotes: The ego can have a tremendous influence on a leader’s choices, decisions, communication, and relationships.
Every leader has an ego. A healthy one provides confidence, conviction, courage, and the ability to make difficult decisions.
The ego-driven leader often confuses the very idea of leadership with having control over everything, including people.
A leader’s greatest challenge is often not managing other people. It is managing themselves by keeping their ego in check.
With an oversized ego, a leader can come to believe the organization exists to support them. This is the antithesis of true leadership.
